subtopic_detail: Planning birth when unprotected foetal vessels are seen crossing the membranes below the presenting part
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29 year old woman at 32 weeks in her first pregnancy, conceived after in vitro fertilisation. Her morphology scan reported a bilobed placenta and a repeat transvaginal scan today has been arranged because of that finding.

The scan shows foetal vessels running through the membranes across the internal os, 1 cm below the presenting part, confirmed as foetal in origin on colour and pulsed wave Doppler. She has had no bleeding and no contractions, the membranes are intact, foetal growth is on the 55th centile and the cardiotocograph is normal. She lives forty minutes from the hospital and has been counselled about the range of birth options by the consultant.

data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non tender, no vaginal bleeding, cephalic presentation
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound showing foetal vessels crossing the internal os within the membranes, bilobed placenta, foetal growth on the 55th centile, cardiotocography normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Admit from about 32 weeks, give corticosteroids, and perform emergency caesarean only if bleeding or labour occurs
options.rationale: Waiting for bleeding means waiting for foetal haemorrhage, and even an immediate response in a fully staffed unit rarely reaches the baby in time because the total foetal blood volume at this gestation is only around 250 mL. Admission is to shorten the response time for the unexpected, not to be the plan. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.text: Manage as an outpatient, give corticosteroids at 36 weeks, and plan caesarean section at 39 weeks before labour
options.rationale: Around a third of women labour or rupture membranes before 37 weeks, and this condition gives no warning and no time to intervene once that happens. Waiting to 39 weeks trades a modest gain in maturity for the specific catastrophe the diagnosis predicts. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.text: Manage as an outpatient, plan induction of labour at 38 weeks, and perform amniotomy under direct vision in theatre
options.rationale: Any plan involving labour exposes the vessels to spontaneous or artificial rupture, and controlled amniotomy does not protect vessels that tear with uterine activity or with the presenting part descending. Vaginal birth is not an option once these vessels are confirmed. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.text: Admit from about 32 weeks, give corticosteroids, and plan caesarean section at 34 to 36 weeks before labour
options.rationale: Unprotected foetal vessels overlying the os rupture when the membranes do, and the foetal blood volume is so small that exsanguination occurs within minutes. Planned abdominal birth before labour, with steroids and inpatient proximity to theatre, converts a condition with very high perinatal mortality into one with survival above 95 percent. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal scan at 36 weeks, and decide on the mode of birth only if the vessels still overlie the os
options.rationale: Unlike a low lying placenta, which migrates as the lower segment forms, vessels running within the membranes do not move away from the os. Building a plan around resolution that does not occur risks the woman labouring while the decision is still open. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia describes foetal vessels running unsupported through the membranes over the internal os, typically arising from a velamentous cord insertion or connecting the lobes of a bilobed or succenturiate placenta. In vitro fertilisation, a low lying placenta in the second trimester and multiple pregnancy all raise the risk, which is why targeted transvaginal colour Doppler is performed when those features appear. When the diagnosis is missed, membrane rupture tears the vessels and the foetus exsanguinates into the vagina, with perinatal mortality historically above half. When it is made antenatally and birth is planned by caesarean before labour, survival exceeds 95 percent. Australian practice is corticosteroids and inpatient admission from around 32 weeks with delivery at 34 to 36 weeks, balancing prematurity against the unpredictable timing of membrane rupture.
key_points: Velamentous cord insertion and bilobed or succenturiate placentas are the substrates
Diagnosis is by transvaginal colour and pulsed wave Doppler confirming foetal vessels
Planned caesarean before labour at 34 to 36 weeks is the management
These vessels do not migrate away from the os as gestation advances
Antenatal diagnosis is the single variable that determines survival
explanation.pearls: Painless vaginal bleeding at membrane rupture with an immediate foetal bradycardia or a sinusoidal trace is foetal blood until proven otherwise and calls for immediate delivery, not for maternal resuscitation, because the mother is haemodynamically well while the baby is the one bleeding.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Vasa praevia

subtopic_detail: Sudden foetal bradycardia with rising station during trial of labour after a previous caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to a 33 year old woman at 40 weeks having a trial of labour after one previous caesarean. She has an epidural in situ and is on a low dose oxytocin infusion for slow progress, and forty minutes ago she was 8 cm dilated with the vertex at station zero.

The cardiotocograph has fallen to a baseline of 80 beats per minute over the past four minutes with no recovery. Her pulse is 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. She reports no pain but feels suddenly unwell and nauseated. On vaginal examination the presenting part is now at station minus 2 and there is fresh blood at the introitus. The uterus feels unusually soft between the infrequent contractions on the tocograph.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 80 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Presenting part risen from station zero to minus 2, fresh vaginal bleeding, uterus soft between contractions, epidural block to T10
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocography showing a prolonged deceleration to 80 beats per minute for four minutes, haemoglobin 112 g/L (115-155) on admission

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Stop the oxytocin, give a tocolytic and reassess the trace over the next ten minutes before deciding
options.rationale: Acute tocolysis is appropriate for a bradycardia caused by uterine hyperstimulation, but the tocograph shows infrequent contractions and a soft uterus, which is the opposite pattern. Spending ten minutes reassessing here uses up the interval in which the baby and the mother are salvageable. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Perform foetal scalp lactate sampling to establish whether the bradycardia reflects significant acidosis
options.rationale: Scalp sampling is invalid during a prolonged deceleration and requires several minutes that this situation does not have. It also answers the wrong question, since the maternal signs already indicate a surgical emergency independent of the foetal blood gas. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum foetal surveillance)

options.text: Attempt an instrumental birth in the room, since she is 8 cm dilated and the head was recently at station zero
options.rationale: She is not fully dilated and the presenting part has risen, so the prerequisites for instrumental birth are absent, and traction on a head that is being displaced by a ruptured uterus worsens the tear. The recent station is a trap because it describes where the head was before the event. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

options.text: Proceed immediately to laparotomy with the neonatal team called and major haemorrhage protocol activated
options.rationale: A prolonged bradycardia with loss of station, fresh bleeding, maternal tachycardia and hypotension during a trial of labour is uterine rupture until proven otherwise, and the only treatment is immediate surgical delivery and repair. Maternal and foetal survival both fall sharply with every ten minutes of delay. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Give a fluid bolus and reposition her to the left lateral, then repeat the vaginal examination in five minutes
options.rationale: Intrauterine resuscitation is correct for a bradycardia caused by aortocaval compression or hypotension after an epidural top up, neither of which explains fresh bleeding and a presenting part that has risen. These measures delay the laparotomy that is the actual treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum foetal surveillance)

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture complicates roughly one in 200 trials of labour after caesarean, and abnormal foetal heart rate patterns, usually a prolonged deceleration or bradycardia, are the presenting feature in the great majority. Classical teaching emphasises scar pain, but working epidurals mask it, so the reliable signs are foetal, haemodynamic and mechanical: sudden bradycardia, maternal tachycardia and hypotension out of proportion to visible loss, fresh vaginal bleeding, loss of the previously recorded station, and cessation of effective contractions. Recognition is the whole task, because the treatment is immediate laparotomy with delivery and repair or, occasionally, hysterectomy. Neonatal outcome deteriorates rapidly beyond about ten to twenty minutes from the onset of the bradycardia, so investigations that add minutes are themselves harmful.
key_points: Abnormal foetal heart rate is the commonest presenting sign of scar rupture
An epidural masks scar pain, so absence of pain is not reassuring
Loss of station and fresh bleeding with maternal tachycardia complete the picture
Immediate laparotomy is the treatment, not further foetal assessment
Contractions often become infrequent and the uterus feels soft after rupture
explanation.pearls: Recheck the station yourself rather than accepting the last documented value, because a presenting part that has risen between two examinations is close to specific for rupture and is the single finding most often missing from the notes of cases reviewed after a poor outcome.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

subtopic_detail: Discordant liquor volumes in a shared placenta twin pregnancy at the mid second trimester
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a maternal foetal medicine clinic reviewing a 26 year old woman at 20 weeks with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy, confirmed by a single placental mass and a T sign at 11 weeks.

Today's scan shows the deepest vertical pocket in the first sac at 1 cm with the bladder not visible, and in the second sac at 9 cm with a distended bladder. The second twin has absent end diastolic flow in the umbilical artery and a normal ductus venosus a wave. Estimated weights are discordant by 18 percent. Both twins have normal anatomy and both have cardiac activity. Her cervix measures 34 mm and she has no contractions.

data_table.Examination: Uterus larger than dates, soft and non tender, cervix closed on ultrasound at 34 mm
data_table.Investigations: Monochorionic diamniotic twins at 20 weeks, deepest vertical pocket 1 cm in twin one with bladder not visualised and 9 cm in twin two with distended bladder, absent end diastolic flow in twin two umbilical artery, estimated weight discordance 18 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange fortnightly growth scans with umbilical artery Dopplers and intervene if the discordance exceeds 25 percent
options.rationale: Growth discordance surveillance is the pathway for selective foetal growth restriction, a different complication of a shared placenta in which liquor volumes stay normal. Here the liquor discrepancy with an absent and a distended bladder defines a condition that progresses over days. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Perform serial amnioreduction from the polyhydramniotic sac and repeat the scan at weekly intervals
options.rationale: Amnioreduction relieves the pressure and prolongs the pregnancy but leaves the anastomoses intact, so the randomised comparison showed worse survival and more neurological injury than laser. It is reserved for gestations beyond the laser window or where laser is unavailable. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Administer maternal corticosteroids and plan delivery of both twins within the next forty eight hours
options.rationale: Delivery at 20 weeks is below the threshold of viability and guarantees the loss of both twins, so it cannot be the response to a treatable condition. Steroids have no role at this gestation. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Perform selective reduction of the smaller twin by cord occlusion to protect the larger twin from injury
options.rationale: Selective reduction is considered when one twin is already severely compromised or has a lethal anomaly and the other is at risk, not as first line when both twins are alive with a treatable vascular imbalance. It forfeits one healthy twin unnecessarily. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Refer for foetoscopic laser ablation of the placental anastomoses at a specialist foetal therapy centre
options.rationale: Laser ablation treats the cause by dividing the vascular connections that drive the transfusion, and it gives higher survival and markedly lower neurological morbidity than drainage for disease at this stage and gestation. Australian practice is urgent referral to one of the small number of centres offering the procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

explanation.summary: Twin to twin transfusion syndrome complicates about one in ten monochorionic pregnancies and arises from unbalanced arteriovenous anastomoses within the shared placenta. Diagnosis rests on the liquor discrepancy alone, defined in Australia as a deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm in one sac and above 8 cm in the other, and staging then follows the Quintero system: stage one is the liquor discrepancy, stage two adds a non visible donor bladder, stage three adds critically abnormal Dopplers, stage four hydrops and stage five death of either twin. Foetoscopic laser ablation divides the offending anastomoses and is the treatment of choice from about 16 to 26 weeks, with survival of at least one twin above 80 percent. Untreated advanced disease carries mortality above 90 percent, so recognition and immediate referral matter more than any bedside intervention.
key_points: Deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm in one sac and above 8 cm in the other defines the condition
A non visible donor bladder and abnormal Dopplers mark advancing Quintero stages
Foetoscopic laser ablation is first line between about 16 and 26 weeks
Amnioreduction gives worse survival and more neurological injury than laser
Selective growth restriction differs because liquor volumes remain normal
explanation.pearls: Establish chorionicity at the first trimester scan and record it in the handheld notes, because a lambda sign at 11 weeks excludes this condition entirely while a T sign commits the woman to fortnightly scanning from 16 weeks, and chorionicity cannot be reliably determined once the second trimester is well advanced.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Twin pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Tense ascites and haemoconcentration in the luteal phase after an assisted reproduction cycle
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar admitting a 31 year old woman nine days after oocyte retrieval and five days after a fresh embryo transfer. She has marked abdominal distension, breathlessness when lying flat, and has passed only 300 mL of urine in the past twelve hours.

Her pulse is 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 percent on room air and temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Her abdomen is tensely distended with shifting dullness, and her calves are soft. Ultrasound shows enlarged ovaries measuring 11 cm bilaterally with gross ascites, and no ovarian torsion on Doppler. Her haematocrit is 0.52, white cell count 18.2 x10^9/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L, sodium 129 mmol/L and albumin 26 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tensely distended abdomen with shifting dullness, reduced air entry at both bases, calves soft and equal
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.52 (0.36-0.46), white cell count 18.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 118 micromol/L (45-90), sodium 129 mmol/L (135-145), albumin 26 g/L (35-50), ultrasound showing 11 cm ovaries with gross ascites and normal Doppler flow

lead_in: Which combination of measures is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous crystalloid, fluid restriction to one litre daily and hypertonic saline for the low sodium level
options.rationale: The hyponatraemia here is dilutional and resolves with correction of the underlying leak, so hypertonic saline treats a number rather than the patient and risks overcorrection. Fluid restriction is directly contrary to the need to refill the intravascular space. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Intravenous crystalloid, prophylactic enoxaparin and laparoscopic ovarian cyst aspiration under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Surgery on friable enlarged ovaries risks haemorrhage and rupture and does nothing for the ascites that is driving her symptoms. Operative intervention is reserved for torsion, rupture with bleeding, or an unrelated surgical diagnosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Intravenous crystalloid, broad spectrum antibiotics and computed tomography of the abdomen for the raised white cell count
options.rationale: Leucocytosis above 15 x10^9/L is characteristic of this syndrome itself and does not indicate infection in an afebrile woman with a clear ultrasound diagnosis. Antibiotics and further imaging delay the drainage and anticoagulation that change the course. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Intravenous frusemide, prophylactic enoxaparin and ultrasound guided paracentesis for the tense ascites
options.rationale: Diuresis in a woman who is intravascularly depleted worsens the haemoconcentration and the acute kidney injury, even though she looks overloaded. Frusemide is considered only after the intravascular compartment has been restored and oliguria persists. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Intravenous crystalloid, prophylactic enoxaparin and ultrasound guided paracentesis for the tense ascites
options.rationale: The pathology is capillary leak with intravascular depletion despite total body fluid overload, so the circulation is refilled while the third space is drained to relieve pressure on the diaphragm and renal veins. Thromboprophylaxis is mandatory because haemoconcentration and high oestradiol make this one of the strongest acquired thrombotic states in gynaecology. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

explanation.summary: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome follows gonadotrophin stimulation and is mediated by vascular endothelial growth factor released from luteinised granulosa cells, producing capillary leak with ascites, pleural effusions and intravascular depletion. Late onset disease appearing more than a week after retrieval is driven by endogenous human chorionic gonadotrophin from an implanting pregnancy and tends to be more severe and more prolonged than the early form. Severity is graded on symptoms, haematocrit, white cell count, renal function and the presence of tense ascites or hydrothorax. Management is supportive and rests on three pillars: intravascular volume replacement, thromboprophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin, and drainage of tense ascites, which relieves dyspnoea and often restores urine output by lowering intra abdominal pressure. Diuretics and surgery both make things worse in the absence of specific indications.
key_points: Capillary leak means intravascular depletion despite visible fluid overload
Late onset disease implies an implanting pregnancy and runs a longer course
Replace volume, anticoagulate, and drain tense ascites
Diuretics worsen haemoconcentration and renal impairment
Leucocytosis is part of the syndrome and does not indicate infection
explanation.pearls: Thrombosis in this syndrome occurs characteristically in the internal jugular and subclavian veins rather than the legs, and can appear weeks after the ascites has resolved, so neck or arm swelling in a woman who had a stimulated cycle in the past two months warrants imaging even if she now feels well.

subtopic_detail: Breakthrough convulsions in the second trimester when the plasma drug concentration has fallen
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar reviewing a 27 year old woman at 22 weeks in her first pregnancy. She has focal epilepsy with secondary generalisation, controlled on lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily and seizure free for three years before conception.

She has had two generalised convulsions in the past fortnight, one while driving her car into the driveway. She has taken every dose, confirmed by her partner and by a dispensing history, and she takes no other medication and no oral contraceptive. She has been on high dose folic acid since before conception. Her plasma lamotrigine concentration is 40 percent below her preconception value, her sodium, calcium, glucose and full blood count are normal, and she has no fever, no headache and no hypertension. Foetal growth and morphology are normal and the cardiotocograph is reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 142 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Fully alert between episodes, no focal neurological deficit, no papilloedema, no hyperreflexia or clonus
data_table.Investigations: Plasma lamotrigine concentration 40 percent below the preconception value, sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), glucose 4.6 mmol/L, haemoglobin 116 g/L (115-155), urine protein negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the lamotrigine dose guided by repeated concentration measurements through the rest of the pregnancy
options.rationale: Oestrogen driven induction of glucuronidation increases lamotrigine clearance markedly from the first trimester, so the same dose produces falling concentrations and breakthrough seizures in an adherent woman. Dosing is adjusted upward against serial levels with a planned reduction in the days after birth as clearance returns to baseline. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Admit for magnesium sulfate and expedite delivery, managing this as an atypical eclamptic presentation
options.rationale: Eclampsia requires hypertension or proteinuria or other features of the disease, and her blood pressure, urinalysis and reflexes are all normal with a known seizure disorder to explain the events. Magnesium is not a treatment for epilepsy. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Switch her to levetiracetam over the coming weeks, with concentrations repeated after the change is complete
options.rationale: Changing agent mid pregnancy exposes the foetus to two drugs during the transition and risks further seizures while neither is at an effective level. Levetiracetam is a reasonable preconception choice but is not the response to a predictable fall in concentration. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Continue the current dose and add clobazam intermittently for clusters, with concentrations repeated each trimester
options.rationale: Adding a second agent increases foetal exposure and side effects without correcting the pharmacokinetic change that caused the breakthrough. The simpler and safer step is to restore the concentration that previously controlled her seizures. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Reduce the lamotrigine dose to limit foetal exposure and manage her seizures with sleep and trigger avoidance
options.rationale: Generalised convulsions carry maternal and foetal risks including trauma, hypoxia, placental abruption and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, all of which outweigh the risk of this drug, which has one of the lowest malformation rates in the class. Reducing the dose inverts the risk balance. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Pregnancy alters the handling of most antiseizure medicines through increased volume of distribution, increased renal clearance, reduced protein binding and, for lamotrigine specifically, strong induction of uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase by rising oestrogen. Lamotrigine clearance can more than double by the third trimester, and the resulting fall in concentration is the commonest reason for seizure deterioration in an adherent woman. Australian practice is to establish a preconception target concentration in a woman who is seizure free, measure at least each trimester, and increase the dose to maintain that individual target rather than to a population range. Seizure control matters because convulsions carry risks of trauma, abruption, foetal hypoxia and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, and driving restrictions apply as they would outside pregnancy. Because clearance falls rapidly after birth, the dose must be brought back down over the first one to two weeks postpartum to avoid toxicity.
key_points: Oestrogen induced glucuronidation markedly increases lamotrigine clearance
Falling concentration is the usual cause of breakthrough seizures in an adherent woman
Set an individual preconception target and measure at least each trimester
Seizure risks to mother and foetus outweigh the risk of this drug
Reduce the dose over one to two weeks after birth as clearance falls
explanation.pearls: Write the postpartum taper on the discharge plan at the time you increase the dose antenatally, because clearance returns towards baseline within days of delivery and a woman left on her third trimester dose typically presents at two weeks with ataxia, diplopia and vomiting from toxicity.
